scenario.prompt_to_agent:
IT and CS Dept users report they cannot reach Server Room
(1.0.0.x) and Internet Lab (128.168.0.x). But Other zone
(192.168.3.x) and Principle Room (192.168.4.x) CAN reach
those targets. router2 shows RIP routes intact and ip_forward
on. Identify what blocks IT/CS but not Other/Principle.

injection.action: add FORWARD DROP rules for IT (192.168.1.0/24) and CS (192.168.2.0/24)
injection.command:
iptables -A FORWARD -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j DROP
  iptables -A FORWARD -s 192.168.2.0/24 -j DROP

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router2 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: New DROP rules block any forwarded packet whose
  source is in 192.168.1.0/24 (IT Dept) or 192.168.2.0/24
  (CS Dept). Office (192.168.3.x) and Principle (192.168.4.x)
  source addresses are not matched, so they are unaffected.
  Routing is healthy; the drop is at the firewall layer.
Localization: router2
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rules for
  192.168.1.0/24 (IT) and 192.168.2.0/24 (CS)
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j DROP && iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.2.0/24 -j DROP` on router2
scenario.fix_spec: remove both DROP rules on router2 — `iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j DROP && iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.2.0/24 -j DROP`

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is a pair of injected firewall rules in the FORWARD chain of **router2** that silently drop all packets whose source address belongs to the IT department subnet (192.168.1.0/24) or the CS department subnet (192.168.2.0/24). The rules exist in both the legacy `iptables` filter table and an `nftables ip filter FORWARD` chain — both active simultaneously, with packet counters of 104 and 6 respectively confirming they have been hit.

**Mechanism:** When an IT or CS host (192.168.1.x / 192.168.2.x) sends traffic toward the Server Room (1.0.0.x) or Internet Lab (128.168.0.x), the packet traverses router0 → router1 → router2. At router2, the packet is presented to the FORWARD chain for eth2→eth0 forwarding. Because the source IP matches one of the two DROP rules, the packet is silently discarded before reaching switch4/switch5 and the end hosts. The same rules also intercept any reply traffic transiting router2 in the other direction with a 192.168.1/2 source (e.g., router2 forwarding return ICMP replies from IT/CS hosts back to the server-side), making the failure bidirectional. Other/Principle hosts (192.168.3/4.x) are not listed in either DROP rule and forward cleanly. IT/CS hosts can still reach router2's own interfaces (INPUT chain, not FORWARD) which explains why pings to 1.0.0.1 and 128.168.0.1 succeed while pings to 1.0.0.5 and 128.168.0.2 fail.

**Root cause:** Malicious or erroneous FORWARD DROP rules were added to router2's netfilter subsystem targeting the IT and CS source subnets.

**Fix:** On router2, remove the two rules:
```
iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.1.0/24 -j DROP
iptables -D FORWARD -s 192.168.2.0/24 -j DROP
nft delete rule ip filter FORWARD handle <it-handle>
nft delete rule ip filter FORWARD handle <cs-handle>
```

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly names router2 as the affected device multiple times and gives fixes to run on router2.
The report explicitly identifies injected firewall DROP rules in router2's FORWARD chain (iptables) and even references removing those iptables FORWARD rules.
The report explicitly states DROP rules matching source subnets 192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.2.0/24 (iptables -s / nft source matches), satisfying the source-filter recognition requirement.
Proposes deleting the two FORWARD DROP rules on router2 (both iptables and corresponding nftables rules), which matches the expected remediation.

The agent's logs show targeted tcpdump captures, routing and rp_filter checks, and an iptables/nft observation that directly locate packet drops on router2's FORWARD path; the writeup's claims follow from those observations and the remediation is appropriate.
